title: Three fields
hookLine: desire, action and assent: the three areas of training (Discourses 3.2)
carry: let each door open for a few breaths

cards: A good gym program doesn't just say get fit. It splits the work: one day legs, one day upper body, one day endurance. You know what you're training today, and why.
A few weeks ago, back on not more books, Epictetus told a proud student to show him his progress in desire, action and judgment.
Now, at the start of book three of the Discourses, he lays out that plan in full: three fields, in order, with a warning about which one people skip to first.

teach.b: This is Discourses book three, chapter two. There are three fields, Epictetus says, in which anyone who wants to be good has to train.
The first is desire and aversion: learning to want and avoid things so that you're never let down by what you want, and never trapped by what you're trying to avoid.
He calls this the most urgent, because it's where the storms come from: grief, envy, fear, the feeling of being thwarted. They all start when a desire misses or an aversion hits.

teach.h: SECOND: ACTION, NOT LIKE A STATUE.
teach.b: The second field is action, our impulses to do or not do: acting in order, thoughtfully, not carelessly. And here's a line that surprises people who think Stoics are cold.

I'm not supposed to be unfeeling like a statue, he says. I'm supposed to keep up my relationships, the ones I was born into and the ones I chose: as a son, a brother, a father, a citizen, someone who honors the gods.
The third field is assent: not being fooled, not agreeing too quickly. This one is for people already making progress, so that their judgment holds even when they're tired, or sad, or half asleep.
And his warning: the philosophers of his day loved to skip straight to the third field, to clever arguments and logic puzzles, while their desires and relationships were a mess.
Start where the storms start, he says. The logic can come later.

how: Many modern Stoic practitioners organize their practice around Epictetus' three fields, sometimes focusing on one per day: desire, action or assent.

games.q: you're a new student, eager to master clever logic puzzles. which field does Epictetus say to start with?
games.why: he calls desire and aversion the most urgent, and says the third field, assent, is for those already making progress.

practice: Hold the three fields in mind like three doors. Desire: what am I wanting or dreading today? Action: who do I owe something to, and how will I act toward them?
Assent: what thought am I likely to believe too quickly? Let each door open for a few breaths, then pick one as your training field.

wordCard.voice: Three fields. Epictetus' training plan: desire and aversion first, then action in our relationships, then assent, the care of our judgments.

orig.note: Greek topos: a place or field (as in topic); Epictetus' word for the three areas of training.

carryVoice: Your line: let each door open for a few breaths. Desire comes first, where the storms start. Until tomorrow.
